production_notes: [VERSION] Which tools offer character or object reference features, and how consistent current models are, must be checked against the live tools before recording. The voiceover says only that some tools offer reference features and that perfect consistency is not always possible.
[REGION] Google Flow availability differs by country; the CTA tells learners they can use Kling for the exercise.
Scene 12 hero clip is generated in Google Flow from Tomás's fixed character description in content.md. The bookseller is a fictional generated character; no readable book titles, signs or logos.

Scenes 13 and 14: for the before-and-after slides, generate Tomás's 3 text-only clips and the 3 keyframe-based clips, and take matching still frames showing the glasses, apron and counter changes listed in content.md.
Tomás and the bookshop in Córdoba are hypothetical; show no real bookshop name or logo.

Hook.voiceover: In shot two, your character wears a blue scarf. In shot three, the scarf is green. In shot four, her hair is shorter. Viewers may not name the problem, but they feel that something is wrong.

Explain.voiceover: In the last two lessons, you generated your first clips. Today, you learn why clips drift apart, and five ways to keep them together.

slide.title: Keeping Characters and Scenes Consistent
slide.body: AI Video Production and Motion · Lesson 8 of 14

Explain.voiceover: Why do clips drift? A video model does not remember your previous clip. Each generation starts again from your prompt, and sometimes an image. Words like a woman in a scarf allow many possible results, so the model chooses a slightly different one each time.

slide.title: Why clips drift
slide.body: One prompt, 'a woman in a scarf', with three arrows to three slightly different women: different scarf colours, hair lengths and faces. Caption: each generation starts again.

Explain.voiceover: The common changes are faces, clothes, colours and light, props, and the setting. A cup becomes a glass. One shot is warm and the next is cool. A window moves to the other wall.

slide.title: What drifts
slide.body: Faces: shape, age, features · Clothes: colours, patterns, accessories · Colours and light: warm then cool · Props: a cup becomes a glass · Setting: a window moves

Explain.voiceover: So how do you reduce drift? The strongest technique for beginners is to reuse keyframes. Start clips from keyframes that already match, as you learned in lesson five. Then use a fixed character description, and paste the same words every time.

slide.title: Reduce drift, part 1
slide.body: 1. Reuse matching keyframes (strongest for beginners) · 2. A fixed character description, pasted word for word

Explain.voiceover: Some tools also let you give a reference image of a character or object to reuse. Use only fictional characters, or images you have the rights to. And keep your style block fixed in every prompt.

slide.title: Reduce drift, part 2
slide.body: 3. Reference features, where the tool offers them: fictional characters or images you have rights to · 4. The same style block in every prompt

Explain.voiceover: The last technique happens in the edit. Cut from a wide shot to a close-up of hands, so a small face change is less visible. Keep shots of the same character short. And avoid placing two very similar shots next to each other.
Explain.stock_query: video editor cutting clips on timeline
Explain.on_screen_text: 5. Hide small changes in the edit

Explain.voiceover: Perfect consistency is not always possible with current tools. Your job is to make the changes small enough that viewers do not notice them.

Film crews have a continuity supervisor. This person photographs every actor and set before each take, so the coffee cup is still half full, and the collar is still open, in the next shot. With AI video, you are your own continuity supervisor.
Explain.stock_query: person taking photos of film set props

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see an example. Tomás runs a bookshop in Córdoba, Argentina. The shop is made up for this lesson. He wants a friendly bookseller character in three shots.
Demonstrate.stock_query: cosy small bookshop interior with wooden shelves

Demonstrate.voiceover: He writes a fixed description. A man in his fifties with short grey hair, a neat grey beard, round black glasses, and a dark green apron over a white shirt.

slide.title: The bookseller
slide.body: A man in his fifties with short grey hair, a neat grey beard, round black glasses, a dark green apron over a white shirt with rolled sleeves.

Demonstrate.voiceover: He generates three clips from text only. The man takes a book from a shelf, reads at a counter, and hands a paper bag to a customer.
Demonstrate.broll_prompt: A man in his fifties with short grey hair, a neat grey beard, round black glasses and a dark green apron over a white shirt with rolled sleeves takes a book from a tall wooden shelf in a small, cosy bookshop; slow dolly-in from medium shot; warm afternoon light through a window; realistic cinematic style, warm natural colours; 6 seconds; no readable book titles, no signs, no text, no logos.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Then he puts them side by side and makes a continuity list. In shot two, the glasses are thinner and gold. In shot three, the apron is dark blue, not green, and the beard is longer. And the counter is wood in one shot, and white in the next.

slide.title: Continuity list
slide.body: Table: Shot 2 · glasses thinner and gold · visible in close-up. Shot 3 · apron dark blue, not green · visible. Shot 3 · beard longer · small. Shots 2–3 · counter wood, then white · visible. Still frames beside each row.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Now his fixes. He generates one keyframe of the bookseller, and uses it as the starting image for all three shots. He adds wooden counter to every prompt. For shot three, he changes the framing to a close-up of hands and the paper bag, so the face is not needed.

slide.title: Three fixes
slide.body: One keyframe of the bookseller → arrows to shots 1, 2 and 3. Tag: 'wooden counter' in every prompt. Shot 3 reframed as a close-up of hands and a paper bag.

Demonstrate.voiceover: The new version has only one small change. He accepts it, because a viewer watching at normal speed is very unlikely to notice it.

slide.title: Before and after
slide.body: Left: three text-only frames with four changes circled. Right: three keyframe-based frames with one small change circled. Tick: accepted.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to check each clip on its own and decide it is good. Continuity problems only appear when clips are next to each other. So always review clips in order, before you decide which ones to keep.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, clips drift because each generation starts again, so faces, clothes, colours, props and settings can change. Second, reused keyframes, a fixed character description, reference features and a fixed style block all reduce drift. Third, review clips in order, and use editing choices to hide small changes you cannot fix.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Each generation starts again, so clips drift. 2. Keyframes, fixed descriptions, references, style block. 3. Review in order; hide small changes in the edit.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. Generate three clips of the same fictional character, in Google Flow or Kling. Put them in order, and list every change you notice, and whether a viewer would notice it. Then choose one technique from this lesson to fix the biggest change. It takes about thirty minutes. Next lesson: Avatar Presenters in HeyGen.
